cue: Reds fade to grey, the water is blue, and each eye looks its own way.
rows: Damselfish, the family of the clownfish, have four kinds of colour-sensing cells, one of them for ultraviolet light, and many wear ultraviolet patterns that they show one another. A triggerfish has three kinds, tuned to violet, blue and green. Neither has a cell tuned to red, so this view darkens reds and adds an invented violet sheen for ultraviolet.

Sea water swallows red light within the first 10 to 20 metres, so deeper down a red fish looks dark grey and a reef turns blue-green. This view tints the picture blue-green and fades reds with distance.

Small reef fish see coarsely. An Ambon damselfish and a dottyback resolved about a fortieth as much detail as you do, though the cells in their eyes are packed tightly enough for about three times more. This view blurs the picture to match.

Wrasses, blennies, pufferfish, triggerfish and seahorses can turn each eye on its own, and each eye has a small sharp centre, called a fovea. One eye can follow a passing fish while the other searches the reef. This view gives each half of the screen its own sharp spot, and the two wander separately.

A squirrelfish, a reef fish that hunts at night, follows a flickering light up to 70 flashes a second in bright light, faster than you can, and only about 40 at night. This view runs slightly slow in daylight and then jumps ahead to catch up.
How fast each eye jumps and how long it stays are the app’s own choices. That the two eyes move independently is measured.
A phone camera can’t measure distance, so this view takes things higher in the picture to be farther away when it fades their reds.
Rows of sensors along a fish’s head and body, called the lateral line, feel the flow and pressure of moving water within one or two body lengths. The picture leaves this sense out.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a threespot damselfish, a black-tailed dascyllus or a blue-green chromis, a review states that you have four kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. If you are a Pomacentrus amboinensis, one of your four kinds senses ultraviolet, which humans cannot see at all, and if you are a lagoon triggerfish, you have three kinds. For most other reef fish, nobody has measured how many kinds you have.
rows.note: Left out R3 and R4 (largemouth bass, a freshwater fish); no record supports carrying its pigment peak or cell count to reef fish. Replaced "reports" with "states" for the voice check.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the few reef fish that have been measured read far fewer. If you are a black-faced blenny, the spacing of the cells in your eye gives 7 to 9, and if you are an Ambon damselfish, a test with striped patterns gave a little over 1. A compilation of earlier measurements lists about 3 for the lagoon triggerfish, 7 for the Koran angelfish and 14 for the red grouper, and nobody has measured most other reef fish.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out R4 (quote gives no value) and R2 (freshwater bass, value and quote disagree). Carried grades are not stated, since figures stay with the measured species.

rows.title: Eyes that move apart
rows.text: If you are a black-faced blenny, your eyes are highly mobile, so you can look around at your surroundings without moving your body. If you are a red-black triplefin, you very likely can too, since it belongs to the same genus. For the other reef fish here, nobody has measured how the eyes move.
rows.note: The record does not say whether the eyes move independently, so the row does not claim it.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and only three reef fish have been measured against that. In bright daylight the spotfin squirrelfish sees flicker up to about 70 flashes a second and the split-banded cardinalfish about 40, and the spiny chromis was measured at about 90. Nobody has measured how fast you see flicker unless you are one of those three.
rows.note: Sydney cardinalfish is graded g from R2, but the row stays at i for the view and names only the three measured species.

rows.title: Moving water
rows.text: In the dark, a Lake Malawi cichlid called Aulonocara stuartgranti can find live prey within about half a body length using its lateral line system. That fish lives in a lake, and nobody has measured how well you sense moving water.
rows.note: Only record is a freshwater cichlid, so the row names it and does not carry its figure to reef fish.
